questions.question: Why is QKᵀ divided by √d_k in attention?
options: To keep dot-product magnitudes from growing with dimension, which would saturate softmax and shrink gradients
To normalize the output vectors to unit length
questions.explanation: For unit-variance components, the dot product's variance grows with d_k.

questions.question: Time complexity of full self-attention in sequence length n (hidden size d)?
questions.explanation: Every token attends to every token; memory is O(n²) for the attention matrix (FlashAttention avoids materializing it).

questions.question: A causal mask in decoder attention:
options: Prevents each position from attending to future positions
questions.explanation: Set scores for j > i to −∞ before softmax.

questions.question: Why do transformers need positional information?
options: Self-attention is permutation-invariant; without positions, word order is invisible
questions.explanation: Sinusoidal, learned, RoPE, or ALiBi add order information.

questions.question: RoPE encodes position by:
options: Appending the position index as a token
Adding a learned vector to each token embedding
Rotating query and key vectors by position-dependent angles so their dot product depends on relative position
questions.explanation: Used by Llama, Qwen, Mistral; extendable with scaling methods (NTK, YaRN).

questions.question: Which architecture family dominates today's general-purpose LLMs?
questions.explanation: Encoder-only models remain strong for embeddings and classification.

questions.question: Temperature T in sampling:
options: Divides logits by T before softmax: T < 1 sharpens the distribution, T > 1 flattens it
Limits the number of output tokens

questions.question: Top-p (nucleus) sampling:
options: Samples from the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability ≥ p
Samples only tokens with probability ≥ p
Always picks the p most likely tokens
questions.explanation: The candidate set adapts to how peaked the distribution is.

questions.question: Chinchilla scaling suggests compute-optimal training uses roughly:
questions.explanation: Production models often train far longer than this because smaller models are cheaper at inference.

questions.question: Approximate training compute for a dense transformer with N parameters on D tokens?
questions.explanation: 2ND forward + 4ND backward. Inference ≈ 2N FLOPs per token.

questions.question: Why are LLMs often bad at counting letters in a word?
options: They see subword tokens, not individual characters
They have no training data about spelling
questions.explanation: 'strawberry' may be 2–3 tokens; character structure is only indirectly learned.

questions.question: What does RLHF add after SFT?
options: Optimizing the model against a reward model trained on human preference comparisons (e.g. with PPO and a KL penalty)
questions.explanation: The KL term keeps the policy close to the SFT model to avoid reward hacking.

questions.question: 'Reasoning models' are commonly trained with:
options: Reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards (e.g. correct math answers, passing unit tests)
questions.explanation: This produces long chains of thought; prompting them needs clear goals more than 'think step by step'.

questions.question: An encoder-only model like BERT is pre-trained with:
options: Masked language modeling (predict masked tokens from both sides)
questions.explanation: Bidirectional context makes it good for classification and embeddings, not open-ended generation.

questions.question: Which best reduces hallucination in a production Q&A assistant?
options: Longer system prompts with more adjectives
RAG with citations, explicit permission to say 'I don't know', and a grounding check
questions.explanation: Combine retrieval, abstention, and verification; measure faithfulness.

questions.question: Why does a low-rank (LoRA) update work well for fine-tuning?
options: Because LLM weights are already low-rank
Task-specific weight changes tend to have low intrinsic rank, so a small B·A captures most of the adaptation
Because it trains the whole model faster
questions.explanation: Few trainable parameters, little forgetting, swappable adapters.

questions.question: CLIP is trained by:
options: Contrastively aligning image and text embeddings from paired data
Generating captions with a decoder only
questions.explanation: Enables zero-shot classification and text-to-image retrieval.

questions.question: Matryoshka embeddings let you:
options: Truncate an embedding to fewer dimensions with modest quality loss
questions.explanation: Useful for cheaper first-pass retrieval with a full-dimension re-score.

questions.question: Pre-norm transformer blocks (norm inside the residual branch, before attention/MLP) are preferred because:
options: They train more stably for deep networks
They remove the need for residual connections
questions.explanation: Post-norm (the original) needs careful warmup and is harder to train deep.

questions.question: Write the attention equation and explain it in one sentence.
questions.answer: Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(QKᵀ/√d_k)·V. Each token's output is a weighted average of value vectors, weighted by how well its query matches each key.

questions.question: List the stages of building a chat LLM.
questions.answer: Pre-training (next-token prediction on trillions of tokens) → optional mid-training/continued pre-training (domain, long context) → SFT on instructions → preference tuning (RLHF/DPO/RLAIF) → often RL with verifiable rewards for reasoning → safety tuning and evals.

questions.question: Multi-head vs multi-query vs grouped-query attention?
questions.answer: MHA: each head has its own Q, K, V. MQA: all heads share one K/V (smallest KV cache, some quality loss). GQA: groups of query heads share K/V (a middle ground; standard in modern LLMs).

questions.question: Why doesn't a 1M-token context window make RAG obsolete?
questions.answer: Cost and latency scale with tokens; recall degrades for information in the middle of long contexts; permissions still need enforcing per user; corpora are often far larger than any window; freshness and citations are easier with retrieval.

questions.question: Name 5 prompting techniques that reliably help.
questions.answer: Clear task + constraints + output format; role/context; few-shot examples; delimiters around untrusted content; step-by-step reasoning (or using a reasoning model); decomposition into sub-prompts; self-consistency; structured output schemas; stable prefix first for caching.

questions.question: What is BPE tokenization?
questions.answer: Byte-Pair Encoding: start from characters/bytes and repeatedly merge the most frequent adjacent pair into a new token, building a subword vocabulary. Balances vocabulary size against sequence length; byte-level BPE can encode any string.
